summary:
SkyFlip is a web app that lets anyone search real NASA SPHEREx infrared images for objects that move or change. You pick any point in the sky, and SkyFlip fetches every picture SPHEREx took of that spot from NASA/IPAC's IRSA archive. It lines them up so stars stay still, then plays them as a flipbook. Anything that moves, like a brown dwarf, a fast star, an asteroid or a comet, jumps from frame to frame.

This fits the "Planet X and SPHEREx" challenge because it uses the method that found Pluto and the cold brown dwarf WISE 0855: comparing images taken at different times. SkyFlip adds tools that make faint motion easier to see. These include difference images, shift-and-add stacking, a ruler that measures speed between visits, Gaia DR3 and AllWISE star overlays, and a 102-colour SPHEREx spectrum. When users spot something, they can flag it, and others can vote "I see it too."

SPHEREx is taking far more pictures than professional astronomers can check by hand. SkyFlip lets students and volunteers search real data for unknown moving objects. A 2-minute guided demo gets beginners started, and everything uses real data, never simulated.
details:
• Accelerating citizen science discoveries: SPHEREx maps the entire sky every six months. That's hundreds of thousands of infrared images, too many for professional astronomers to check one by one. SkyFlip turns that archive into something anyone can search. Pick any spot in the sky and SkyFlip pulls every SPHEREx visit to it from NASA/IPAC's IRSA archive, lines the images up so stars stay fixed, and plays them as a flipbook where anything moving jumps out. Difference images cancel out the still stars and leave moving objects as bright/dark pairs. Shift-and-add stacking with adjustable drift brings out objects too faint to see in a single frame. Every picture downloaded is cached for all users, so each new volunteer extends a shared search instead of repeating someone else's. That's how SkyFlip scales the hunt for Kuiper Belt Objects, fast-moving interstellar visitors, and possibly the long-sought Planet Nine / Planet X.
    • Uncovering the solar neighbourhood's missing population: Many of the Sun's closest neighbours are probably still undiscovered: cold T- and Y-type brown dwarfs, too dim in visible light for most surveys to catch. SPHEREx is unusually well suited to finding them. It splits light into 102 infrared colours from 0.75 to 5 µm, covering the exact bands where methane (CH₄) and water (H₂O) absorb light in these objects' atmospheres. SkyFlip puts that power in users' hands. A methane narrow filter highlights these signatures. A spectrum chart shows the light from any spot with common absorption and emission lines marked. A built-in ruler measures how far and how fast an object moves between visits, the key clue that it's nearby. Our welcome flipbook shows WISE 0855, the coldest brown dwarf known, crossing the frame in real SPHEREx data. It's proof that the method works, and an invitation to find the next one.
    • Bridging public volunteers and professional astronomy: Citizen science only matters if its results are trustworthy enough for professionals to act on. SkyFlip is built for that. With one click, users can overlay Gaia DR3 and AllWISE stars to check whether a "discovery" is already known. Known brown dwarf candidates and common artefacts like diffraction spikes are labelled, which removes the most frequent false alarms before anyone flags them. Every flag is saved to a shared database, where other users can independently confirm it with "I see it too", so the community acts as a first review. Candidates that hold up can be exported in the standard Minor Planet Center (MPC) format. The result is a pre-filtering pipeline that hands professionals a short list of vetted, well-measured candidates worth follow-up time on telescopes like JWST or Keck.
    • Democratizing STEM education: SkyFlip brings real space science into classrooms and living rooms anywhere in the world. There are no simulations and no sample data: students and enthusiasts explore the same new SPHEREx images that researchers are analysing right now, and anything they find could be genuinely new. A 2-minute guided demo walks beginners through spotting a real moving streak. It recreates the "blink comparison" method Clyde Tombaugh used to discover Pluto in 1930, now with modern infrared data. The app installs with a single setup script, needs no accounts or keys, runs in any browser, and offers keyboard shortcuts and colour themes. That keeps the barrier to real discovery as low as possible, and it gives the next generation a hands-on reason to care about space exploration.

Programming Languages & Frameworks:

• Frontend: JavaScript (ES6+), React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, HTML5 Canvas API (for high-performance image projection and interactive coordinate rulers).

• Backend: Python 3.9+, FastAPI (asynchronous REST API service), Uvicorn (ASGI server), Pydantic (data modeling).

Astronomical Libraries & Scientific Computation:

• Astropy: Celestial coordinate conversions (Sexagesimal ↔ Decimal degrees, WCS transformations, SkyCoord), FITS data handling.

• Reproject: High-fidelity celestial image reprojection onto common North-Up WCS projections.

• NumPy & SciPy: Array manipulation, difference matrix calculations (B - A), custom bipolar colormap scaling, and shift-and-add co-addition algorithms.

• Pillow (PIL) & Matplotlib: Multi-band color composite generation, contrast stretching, and normalized image rendering.

External Astronomical Services & Data Repositories:

• NASA / IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA): SPHEREx DR1/QR3 multi-epoch cutouts, calibration metadata, and TAP query services.

• NASA / STScI & CDS HiPS Servers: Progressive all-sky HEALPix streaming tiles for optical (DSS2 Color) and infrared (SPHEREx DR1 first layer).

• ESA Gaia DR3 & NASA AllWISE: Cross-matching queries for astrometry, proper motion, parallax, and contamination flags (cc_flags, RUWE).

Database, Cloud & Infrastructure:

• Supabase: Managed PostgreSQL database for user projects, candidate discovery pins, and community votes.

• Supabase Storage: High-availability object storage bucket for caching processed FITS cutouts and rendered PNG/NPY frames.

• Development & Deployment: Git & GitHub, PowerShell, Unix Bash, and Windows batch automated setup scripts. No specialized hardware is required—runs efficiently on standard consumer computers and servers.
